title: What is defineModel() in Vue 3.4+ and how does it replace manual prop + emit?
description: Explain the defineModel macro for two-way binding in script setup.
answer:
**TL;DR:** defineModel() is a script-setup compiler macro that declares a v-model prop and its update event in one line — no manual prop + emit boilerplate.
Before Vue 3.4 a writable `v-model` required `defineProps<{modelValue:string}>()` plus `defineEmits<{ 'update:modelValue':[v:string]}>()` and a computed getter/setter forwarding the emit. `defineModel()` collapses this into a single `Ref`. It returns a writable `ref` that reads the prop and writes by emitting `update:modelValue` automatically. Named models `defineModel('title')` map to `v-model:title`, and `defineModel({ default:0 })` supplies a default. Modifiers (`.trim`, custom `get`/`set` via `defineModel` options) are handled by the second arg `{ get, set }` just like `defineProps` transformers. Under the hood the compiler desugars it to the old prop + emit pair so there is zero runtime cost. | Aspect | Manual prop+emit | `defineModel()` | |---|---|---| | Declaration | 6-8 lines (prop + emit + computed) | 1 line `const m = defineModel()` | | Writable | computed get/set needed | returned ref is directly writable | | Named models | `v-model:foo` needs separate prop/emit | `defineModel('foo')` | | Modifiers | manual parsing | built-in `{ get,set }` + `modifiers` | **Interview Tip:** If asked to build a custom input, write `const model = defineModel({ required:true })` and bind `` — mention you never import it and it is compile-time sugar. ```vue ```

title: What is Vapor mode in Vue 3.5+ and how does it differ from the virtual DOM?
description: Explain Vapor mode's compile strategy and when to use it.
answer:
**TL;DR:** Vapor mode compiles templates to fine-grained, VDOM-free imperative DOM operations with surgical updates — same reactivity, no diffing.
Vue's classic renderer creates a virtual-DOM tree each render and diffs it. Vapor (experimental since 3.4, stabilized opt-in in 3.5) adds a compile flag `vapor:true` that makes `compile()` emit plain JavaScript that inserts real DOM nodes and creates a `ReactiveEffect` per dynamic binding. There is no `h()` or VNode allocation on update — the effect writes directly to the DOM node (`el.textContent = value`). Benchmarks show 2-3x faster mount for static-heavy UIs and ~40% smaller runtime for Vapor-only builds. It reuses the same `ref`/`reactive`/`computed` APIs, so component logic is unchanged. Trade-off: Vapor components cannot use render functions that return VNodes and some advanced custom renderer features. Mixed mode (VDOM + Vapor components interoperate) is supported so you migrate leaf components first. | Aspect | Virtual DOM | Vapor mode | |---|---|---| | Update work | diff entire subtree, patch | direct effect writes to bound node | | Memory | VNode objects per render | none (DOM only) | | Bundle | full runtime (~35kb) | vapor runtime (~14kb) | | Compat | all features | no manual `h()` / some directives limited | **Interview Tip:** Say: 'Vapor is a compiler stratagem, not a new framework — add `defineComponent({ vapor:true })` or `vapor` SFC flag to hot spots and keep shared reactivity.' Mention it pairs with lazy hydration. ```vue // vite.config.ts import { defineConfig } from 'vite' import vue from '@vitejs/plugin-vue' export default defineConfig({ plugins: [vue({ features: { vapor: true } })] }) // Counter.vapor.vue (opt-in per component) ```

title: useId() vs getCurrentInstance() — how do you generate SSR-safe IDs in Vue 3.5?
description: Compare the stable ID helper with manual instance access.
answer:
**TL;DR:** useId() returns an SSR-stable, hydration-safe id per component; getCurrentInstance() is an internal escape hatch you should avoid in app code.
Hydration mismatches occur when server-rendered `id="el-1"` differs from the client's random id. `useId()` (added Vue 3.5, inspired by React) generates a deterministic id scoped to the component tree, consistent across server and client: it uses the component's SSR context and tree position, auto-prefixed to avoid collisions. `getCurrentInstance()` returns the internal component instance (`uid`, `vnode`, `provides`, `appContext`). It exists for library authors (e.g. `vue-router` internals) but is not stable semver and bypasses `script setup` encapsulation. In production builds it can be nulled by tree-shaking. Use `useId()` for label/input `for`/`id` pairing, `aria-describedby`, and any SSR-rendered id. Reserve `getCurrentInstance` for advanced plugins and devtools. | Need | Correct API | Why | |---|---|---| | SSR-stable id for a11y | `useId()` | deterministic, hydration-safe | | Access props / slots programmatically | `defineProps` / `useSlots()` helpers | public, typed | | Library needing instance uid | `getCurrentInstance()?.uid` | last resort, internal | **Interview Tip:** Say: 'For accessibility inputs I call `const id = useId()` and bind `:id="id"` + `:for="id"`; I never ship `getCurrentInstance().uid` — it's undocumented and breaks between minors.' ```vue ```

title: When should you choose Vapor over VDOM in a real app — trade-offs?
description: Explain migration strategy and interop limits for Vapor.
answer:
**TL;DR:** Use Vapor for leaf-heavy, static-heavy components needing max speed; keep VDOM for dynamic render-function libraries.
Vapor's win is proportional to template staticity and update granularity. A marketing page or data grid where each cell updates independently gets near-vanilla-JS performance because each `{{ cell }}` is an isolated effect rather than a VNode re-render. The runtime is also ~50% smaller, useful for embedded widgets. Limitations: no `h()`/JSX returning VNodes inside a Vapor component, limited support for some directive hooks that expect VNodes, and custom renderers (e.g. `vue-threejs`) still require VDOM. Vue allows mixing: a Vapor parent can render a VDOM child and vice versa via interop wrapper. Strategy: profile with `vue-perf` — port the top 5 hot leaf components to Vapor behind a flag, measure INP/LCP, then expand. | Criterion | Vapor | VDOM | |---|---|---| | Static ratio high? | big win | moderate | | Needs render fn / JSX lib? | not yet | yes | | Bundle budget tight? | smaller | larger | | Incremental? | mix allowed | default | **Interview Tip:** Answer the trade-off question with 'benchmark, not ideology — Vapor is opt-in compiler output, so I A/B the hot path in Lighthouse before committing.' ```vue ```

title: watch vs watchEffect — flush timing and the new watch options in 3.5?
description: Compare explicit vs auto-tracked watchers and flush modes.
answer:
**TL;DR:** watch tracks explicit sources with old/new values; watchEffect auto-tracks and runs immediately — control flush with 'pre' | 'post' | 'sync'.
`watch(source, cb, { deep, immediate, flush })` watches a specific getter/ref and calls `cb(newVal, oldVal)` only when that source changes — minimal reruns. `watchEffect(() => { use(state.value) })` runs immediately, tracks every reactive read inside, and re-runs when any of them change. Vue 3.5 adds `watch(..., { once:true })` to auto-stop after first trigger and improves deep-watch performance via shallow dirty check. `flush:'pre'` (default) runs before component render, `'post'` after DOM patch (good for measuring DOM), `'sync'` synchronously (rare, e.g. for custom revert). Rule: use `computed` for derived values, `watch` for async side effects with known sources, `watchEffect` for multi-dep syncing only when deps are too dynamic to list. | Watcher | Trigger | Old value | Use when | |---|---|---|---| | `watch` | explicit source change | yes | fetch on id change | | `watchEffect` | any read reactive change | no | sync multiple deps, logging | **Interview Tip:** Say: 'I default to watch with explicit sources for network calls, and reserve watchEffect for when the dep set is truly dynamic — and I set flush:post when I need DOM measurements.' ```vue ```

title: How do you diagnose and fix hydration mismatches in Vue SSR / Nuxt 3?
description: Explain causes and fixes for SSR hydration warnings.
answer:
**TL;DR:** Mismatch = server HTML != client VDOM — caused by browser-only APIs, random values, or time — fix with ClientOnly or onMounted guards.
During hydration Vue compares server-rendered HTML with the client's first render. Differences from `new Date()`, `Math.random()`, `window.innerWidth`, or `useId` drift trigger `[Vue warn] Hydration mismatch`. Fixes: wrap browser-only UI in `` (Nuxt) or guard with `const mounted = ref(false); onMounted(()=>mounted.value=true)` and `v-if="mounted"`. For ids use `useId()`. For intentional text diff, Vue 3.5 adds `data-allow-mismatch` attribute hint. Lazy hydration `defineAsyncComponent({ hydrate: 'visible' })` also defers mismatch-prone subtrees. Diagnose by comparing View Source vs Elements panel; the warning pinpoints the node. | Mismatch source | Fix | |---|---| | `Date.now()` / `Math.random()` | compute in `onMounted` or provide from server | | `window` / `matchMedia` | guard with `if (import.meta.client)` or `ClientOnly` | | Random id | `useId()` | | Intentional | `data-allow-mismatch` (3.5) | **Interview Tip:** Say: 'I treat hydration warnings as errors in CI — I search for client-only APIs in setup and hoist them to onMounted or ClientOnly.' ```vue ```

title: What is lazy hydration in Vue 3.5 — hydrate strategies (idle, visible, interaction)?
description: Explain defineAsyncComponent hydrate strategies for SSR performance.
answer:
**TL;DR:** Lazy hydration delays hydrating an SSR subtree until idle/visible/interaction — cutting JS and INP.
Vue 3.5 ships `defineAsyncComponent` hydration strategies inspired by Astro/Nuxt: `defineAsyncComponent({ loader:()=>import('./Heavy.vue'), hydrate:'visible' })` tells the SSR renderer to emit static HTML but skip hydrating that subtree until the strategy fires. Options: `'idle'` (after `requestIdleCallback`), `'visible'` (IntersectionObserver), `'interaction'`/`'media'`/`'always'`. This slashes hydration JS: below-fold comments hydrate only when scrolled into view, modals on first interaction. Vapor + lazy hydration is ideal for content-heavy pages. Nuxt 3.11 exposes it as ``. Trade-off: unhydrated subtree is non-interactive until triggered — add `loading` placeholder. | Strategy | Hydrates when | Best for | |---|---|---| | `hydrate: 'idle'` | browser idle | secondary widgets | | `hydrate: 'visible'` | enters viewport | below-fold sections | | `hydrate: 'interaction'` | first click/hover/focus | modal, tooltip | | none (default) | immediately | critical UI | **Interview Tip:** Say: 'I mark below-fold heavy islands as hydrate:visible and measure TTI drop — interactive code only loads when observed.' ```vue ```

title: How does defineAsyncComponent work with loading, error and retry in 2025?
description: Explain options for code-split async components beyond Suspense.
answer:
**TL;DR:** defineAsyncComponent wraps a dynamic import with loading/error components, delay/timeout, and retry — complementing Suspense.
`defineAsyncComponent({ loader:()=>import('./Heavy.vue'), loadingComponent:Spinner, delay:200, timeout:10000, errorComponent:Err, onError(retry,fail,retries){ if(retries<3) retry() } })` gives fine-grained UX: `delay` avoids flashing spinner on fast loads, `timeout` fails slow networks, `onError` retries with backoff. Without `Suspense`, the async component renders loading/error inline. Inside `Suspense`, set `suspensible:true` (default) to let the parent Suspense show its fallback instead of the component's loading. Combine with `import()` magic comments `/* webpackChunkName */` and `` for streaming. | Option | Purpose | |---|---| | `loader` | dynamic import Promise | | `loadingComponent` + `delay` | spinner after threshold | | `errorComponent` + `timeout` | error UI after deadline | | `onError` | retry logic | **Interview Tip:** Say: 'I wrap route components with defineAsyncComponent + Suspense — delay 200ms avoids spinner flash, and onError retries transient chunk failures.' ```vue ```

title: When should you use readonly, markRaw, and toRaw in Vue reactivity?
description: Explain opting out or protecting reactive state.
answer:
**TL;DR:** readonly blocks mutations (warn), markRaw opts object out of reactivity forever, toRaw unwraps the proxy.
`readonly(obj)` returns a reactive proxy that warns (dev) and no-ops on mutation while still tracking reads for derived computed — ideal for `provide(readonly(state))` so consumers cannot mutate parent state. `markRaw(obj)` flags an object to never be proxied even if passed to `reactive`/`ref`. Use for large external instances (Mapbox `Map`, Three.js `Mesh`) or class instances with internal invariants that break under proxy. `toRaw(proxy)` returns the underlying raw object — needed when interacting with non-Vue code that checks identity (`map.has(toRaw(obj))`) or serializes to JSON without proxy traps. | API | Effect | Mutations | |---|---|---| | `readonly(o)` | reactive proxy, Warn on write | blocked (warn) | | `markRaw(o)` | never proxied | allowed (non-reactive) | | `toRaw(p)` | unwrap proxy | bypasses reactivity | **Interview Tip:** Say: 'I provide readonly(state) to children so they consume but cannot write, and markRaw vendor instances to avoid proxy overhead.' ```vue ```
